title: The Horn, the Fire, and the Righteous

paragraphs.text: This passage opens with a powerful picture of the Day when the Horn is blown. On that Day, people will not come out alone; they will come forth in multitudes, great crowds, one group after another. The whole universe will change in ways that are hard to imagine. The heaven will be opened, and it will become like many gates. The mountains, which seem so solid and permanent to us now, will be removed, and they will become nothing more than a mirage, like the false image of water that a traveler sees in the desert heat.

Then the ayahs turn to Hell, which has been lying in wait, as if watching for those who crossed the limits. It will be their place of return, and they will stay in it for ages without end. There they will find no coolness to comfort them and nothing pleasant to drink. They will taste only scalding water and foul pus, which is a fitting recompense for what they did. The reason is made clear: they never expected that they would have to give an account of their deeds, and they denied Allah's verses with strong, stubborn denial. However, nothing was forgotten, because Allah has counted and recorded everything in writing. They will be told to taste the penalty, and they will be given nothing more except greater torment. These words are a serious warning, and they remind the reader that every action is written down and that denial does not make the account disappear.

After this frightening scene, the passage gives a very different picture for the righteous, who were mindful of Allah. For them there is real success and attainment. They will have gardens and grapevines, companions of equal age, and a cup that is always full. The contrast between the two groups is sharp and clear. One group meets burning water and endless pain, while the other receives gardens, fellowship and plenty. In this way, the ayahs invite the reader to think carefully about which path he is choosing in this life, while there is still time to prepare for that Day.
